3	> Working agreements for everyone (human and AI) writing code in this repo. These rules are locked in Week 1 and override any "speed > quality" temptation. If a week's exit gate conflicts with them, **the rules win**.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## A. Commit & change discipline
8	
9	1. **One functionality per commit** (where possible). Each commit must be independently reviewable; do not bundle two unrelated changes.
10	
11	   **1a. Every functionality change ships with test coverage** — unit/integration as applicable. Enforced by the ≥80% CI gate (rule 13/14) since the Week-8 flip (2026-07-03); this is no longer a "from Week 8" aspiration, it's live and blocking.
12	   **1b. Update docs in the same PR if the change is user-facing or architectural** — CLAUDE.md, the relevant ADR, CONTRIBUTING.md, or user docs, whichever applies.
13	   **1c. Every PR gets an agentic code review before merge.** Spawn `/code-review` (never an inline self-review only), and post its findings to the PR as inline comments (`/code-review --comment`). Fix what it finds in the same PR where feasible; anything genuinely deferred must be filed as a GitHub issue (rule 3) — never dropped silently.
14	2. **Manually test each committed change before starting the next functionality**, in addition to automated coverage. "Tested" means: the affected code path was exercised locally, not just that it compiled.
15	3. **Defects → GitHub issue first, never silent fixes.** Use `gh issue create --title "fix: <desc>"`. The PR that fixes it must include `Fixes #N` in the title or body. This also covers findings deferred out of a `/code-review` pass (rule 1c).
16	4. **Every new functionality ships with unit tests.** Tests live next to the code they cover (`backend/tests/`, `frontend/tests/`).
17	
18	   **4a. ---
name: dev-subagents-share-your-git-worktree
description: "A subagent that checks out a branch moves YOUR HEAD — commits then land on the wrong branch; give review agents worktree isolation or read-only instructions"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
---

Subagents run in the **same working tree** as the main thread unless launched with
`isolation: "worktree"`. So a review/verification agent that runs `git checkout`
silently moves the main thread's HEAD.

**How it bit (2026-07-25):** a background PR-review agent created a `pr984-check`
branch and checked out `main` to diff against. Meanwhile the main thread was
mid-edit on `fix/triage-frontend-batch` with uncommitted frontend work. The next
`git add -A && git commit` therefore committed that work **onto local `main`**,
not the feature branch. It looked like the changes had vanished: the feature
branch was at its base commit, `git status` showed only an unrelated file, and a
`git reset --soft HEAD~1` on the feature branch then rewound it *below* its base.

**How to find it:** `git reflog` is the whole story — look for `checkout: moving
from <agent-branch> to main` entries you never issued, and for your `commit:`
entry sitting directly after one. `git branch -v` shows the stranded work as
`main [ahead 1]`. Nothing is lost; the commit is intact.

**Recovery:** `git reset --hard origin/main` on the feature branch (or
`checkout -B <branch> origin/main`), `git cherry-pick --no-commit <stranded-sha>`
to bring the tree back, then `git branch -f main origin/main` to repair local main
**without checking it out** (you cannot check it out while the restored changes are
uncommitted).

**How to apply:**
- Launch any agent that might touch git state with `isolation: "worktree"`, or
  instruct it explicitly to run read-only git commands only — no `checkout`, no
  branch creation.
- **Commit or stash before spawning** a background agent that inspects a PR.
- Treat "my changes disappeared" as a reflog question first, never as data loss.

This is the same family as the earlier incident where a branch switch swept #591's
files into the #904 branch, and as [[feedback-shared-playwright-session]] — one
shared resource, two actors, no locking. See also
[[dev-stacked-pr-after-squash-merge]] for the other git-state trap in this repo.

"""#457 — trip-wire for partial-index / predicate drift across OrchestrationProviders.

The trigger-dedup unique index on `runs` is PARTIAL: it only covers rows whose
`triggered_by` carries an orchestration prefix. That predicate is spelled in three
places — the model's `__table_args__`, the migration that created it, and the
service constant used for the `ON CONFLICT` upsert — and all three must list every
provider in `ORCHESTRATION_PROVIDERS`.

Adding a provider without widening them is silent: dedup simply stops applying to
the new provider's runs, so a re-delivered webhook creates a duplicate run instead
of being rejected. Nothing fails, nothing logs — you find out from duplicate rows.

dbt (ADR 0029) was added and the widening WAS done by hand (migration
`c1d2e3f4a5b6`), which is exactly why this guard is worth having: it worked that
time, and there was no test that would have noticed if it hadn't.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re

from backend.app.db.models import ORCHESTRATION_PROVIDERS, Run
from backend.app.services.orchestration_service import _ORCH_TRIGGER_PREDICATE

_PREFIX_RE = re.compile(r"triggered_by LIKE '([a-z_]+):%'")


def _covered_prefixes(predicate_sql: str) -> set[str]:
    return set(_PREFIX_RE.findall(predicate_sql))


def _model_predicate() -> str:
    for arg in Run.__table_args__:
        if getattr(arg, "name", None) == "uq_runs_suite_triggered_by":
            return str(arg.dialect_options["postgresql"]["where"])
    raise AssertionError("uq_runs_suite_triggered_by is missing from Run.__table_args__")


def test_model_partial_index_covers_every_orchestration_provider() -> None:
    """The dedup index's predicate must name every provider — no more, no fewer."""
    assert _covered_prefixes(_model_predicate()) == set(ORCHESTRATION_PROVIDERS)


def test_service_upsert_predicate_covers_every_orchestration_provider() -> None:
    """The `ON CONFLICT` predicate must match the index it targets.

    Postgres only uses a partial unique index for conflict resolution when the
    statement's `index_where` matches it, so a service predicate that drifts from
    the model's turns the upsert into a plain insert — duplicates, no error.
    """
    assert _covered_prefixes(str(_ORCH_TRIGGER_PREDICATE)) == set(ORCHESTRATION_PROVIDERS)


def test_model_and_service_predicates_agree() -> None:
    """Stated separately from the two above so a failure says WHICH drifted."""
    assert _covered_prefixes(_model_predicate()) == _covered_prefixes(str(_ORCH_TRIGGER_PREDICATE))

def test_list_pipeline_runs_rejects_an_unknown_provider(
    client: TestClient, db_session: Any
) -> None:
    """A typo'd provider must 422, not return a confident empty list (#306).

    The pre-fix behaviour was `200 []` — indistinguishable from "this provider has
    no runs", which is the confidently-empty-answer class (#828). Seed a real run
    first so an empty body could ONLY come from the filter, never from an empty
    table.
    """
    owner = _user(db_session, "owner@ex")
    _pipeline_run(db_session, owner, provider="adf", status="succeeded")
    _as(owner)

    resp = client.get("/api/v1/pipeline_runs?provider=ADF")  # right name, wrong case
    assert resp.status_code == 422
    assert "adf" in resp.json()["detail"]["detail"]["allowed"]

    assert client.get("/api/v1/pipeline_runs?provider=nope").status_code == 422
    # The valid value still works, and still returns the seeded row.
    assert len(client.get("/api/v1/pipeline_runs?provider=adf").json()) == 1
    # Omitting the filter is not "unknown" — it means no filter.
    assert client.get("/api/v1/pipeline_runs").status_code == 200

) -> None:

    _pipeline_run(db_session, owner, provider="adf", status="succeeded")

    resp = client.get("/api/v1/orchestration/pipelines?env=production")  # real env is "prod"

    assert "prod" in resp.json()["detail"]["detail"]["allowed"]
    assert client.get("/api/v1/orchestration/pipelines?provider=adf&env=dev").status_code == 200

log = get_logger(__name__)

# Predicate of the partial unique index `uq_runs_suite_triggered_by` (#308) —
# kept identical to the migration and the model's `postgresql_where`. Scopes the
# dedup guard to orchestration markers (`<provider>:<pipeline>:<run_id>`) so the
# repeatable manual/probe/schedule markers are unaffected.
_ORCH_TRIGGER_PREDICATE = text(
    "triggered_by LIKE 'adf:%' OR triggered_by LIKE 'airflow:%' OR triggered_by LIKE 'dbt:%'"
)

# Terminal pipeline-run statuses — a run in one of these won't transition again,
# so the poll's `skip_updated_since` churn-optimisation may skip re-recording it.
# A non-terminal row (queued/running) must always be re-processed so a later
# transition (e.g. running → succeeded) isn't dropped (#490).

def test_build_mcp_app_allowlists_proxied_hosts(monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    """FastMCP's transport guard defaults to loopback-only hosts and 421s anything
    else — but DataQ always fronts the api with the nginx proxy, which forwards the
    upstream Host (the ACA FQDN in prod, `api` in compose). Assert build_mcp_app
    passes those hosts so the guard can't shadow the real auth gate."""
    captured: dict[str, Any] = {}
    monkeypatch.setattr(server, "mcp_enabled", lambda: True)
    monkeypatch.setattr(server.mcp, "http_app", lambda **kw: captured.update(kw) or "APP")

    assert server.build_mcp_app() == "APP"
    hosts = captured["allowed_hosts"]
    assert "*.azurecontainerapps.io" in hosts  # prod (internal api FQDN)
    assert "api" in hosts  # docker-compose upstream
    # Origins are relaxed for the same reason (Bearer-token auth → no CSRF), so a
    # browser client (claude.ai) isn't 403'd by the guard's separate Origin check.
    assert captured["allowed_origins"] == ["*"]


def test_allowed_hosts_match_prod_and_compose_upstreams() -> None:
    """Prove the allowlist patterns actually match the real proxied Host values —
    so the mount doesn't 421 in prod (regression guard for the 3.4.3 DNS-rebind
    guard). Uses stdlib `fnmatchcase`, exactly what FastMCP's `_host_matches` uses,
    without coupling the test to that private helper."""
    from fnmatch import fnmatchcase

    def matches(host: str, patterns: list[str]) -> bool:
        return any(p == "*" or fnmatchcase(host, p) for p in patterns)

    hosts = ["*.azurecontainerapps.io", "api", "localhost", "127.0.0.1"]
    # The exact prod upstream nginx forwards (DATAQ_API_UPSTREAM, internal ingress);
    # fnmatch `*` spans dots, so the wildcard matches the multi-label FQDN.
    assert matches(
        "dataq-app-api.internal.purplefield-f7322a1b.westus2.azurecontainerapps.io", hosts
    )
    assert matches("api", hosts)  # docker-compose
    assert not matches("evil.example.com", hosts)  # still rejects the rest

def test_allowed_hosts_come_from_settings_not_hardcoded(monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    """A non-ACA deployment can configure the allowlist (#728).

    The list used to be a literal in `build_mcp_app`, which is the one deploy-target
    coupling ADR 0010/0013 forbids in app code: any proxy forwarding a different
    upstream Host (EKS/GKE, on-prem, a renamed compose service) got a 421 with no
    way to fix it short of a code change.
    """
    from backend.app.core import config

    captured: dict[str, Any] = {}
    monkeypatch.setattr(server, "mcp_enabled", lambda: True)
    monkeypatch.setattr(server.mcp, "http_app", lambda **kw: captured.update(kw) or "APP")

    settings = config.get_settings()
    monkeypatch.setattr(settings, "mcp_allowed_hosts", "*.example.internal, dataq-api ")
    config.get_settings.cache_clear()
    monkeypatch.setattr(config, "get_settings", lambda: settings)
    monkeypatch.setattr(server, "get_settings", lambda: settings)

    server.build_mcp_app()

    # Whitespace stripped, order preserved, and the ACA default fully replaced —
    # not merged, so an operator can genuinely narrow the allowlist.
    assert captured["allowed_hosts"] == ["*.example.internal", "dataq-api"]

monitors: list[MonitorSpec],
    now: datetime,
) -> list[CheckOutcome]:
    """Band a list of monitors given a per-spec scalar source, one ``CheckOutcome``
    each, in order. ``scalar_for`` returns the monitor's scalar (``MAX(column)`` /
    ``COUNT(*)``) — the only datasource-specific bit: a SQL runner builds+runs a
    query (`evaluate_monitors`), the Iceberg runner computes it natively
    (``scan().count()`` / a column ``MAX``). DB-free and unit-testable.

    A monitor that can't be evaluated — bad column/range (config error) or its
    scalar source raised (e.g. unknown column) — yields an ``errored`` outcome for
    *that* check only; its siblings still run (mirrors `CheckRunner`'s per-check
    `error`, #122). The scalar source must **not** swallow a datasource-establishment
    failure (open connection / load catalog): callers do that before the loop so it
    propagates and fails the whole run."""
    outcomes: list[CheckOutcome] = []
    for spec in monitors:
        try:
            outcomes.append(
                monitor_outcome(spec.kind, scalar=scalar_for(spec), config=spec.config, now=now)
            )

def test_monitor_error_message_never_carries_raw_exception_text() -> None:
    """A per-monitor failure must not write the driver's message into a result row (#900).

    `error_message` flows into `results.observed_value` -> the run-detail API -> the
    UI. That sink never passes the logger-level scrubber (CLAUDE.md §10 protects
    logs, not DB columns), and Azure storage exceptions embed the full SAS-signed
    URL in their text (#828) — so a raw `str(exc)` here persists a live credential
    where any viewer of the run can read it.

    Asserted on the pipeline, not on the classifier: this is the #849 lesson —
    testing the scrub helper proves nothing about the path that forgot to call it.
    """
    secret = "REDACTED%3D"

    def fetch(_statement: Any) -> object:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"HttpResponseError: server failed to authenticate; "
            f"https://acct.blob.core.windows.net/c/o?se=2027-01-01&{secret}"
        )

    out = evaluate_monitors(
        fetch,
        table="T",
        schema=None,
        catalog=None,
        monitors=[MonitorSpec(kind="volume", config={"min_rows": 1})],
    )

    assert out[0].errored is True
    message = out[0].error_message or ""
    assert secret not in message
    assert "sig=" not in message
    assert "blob.core.windows.net" not in message
    # And it still says something useful rather than being blanked.
    assert message.strip()

1	"""Flat-file (ADLS Gen2 / S3) IO + GX `CheckRunner`.
2	
3	Two responsibilities for the flat-file datasources, both behind the same
4	primitives the SQL adapters use (raw config dict + resolved secret, never the ORM
5	row — keeps `datasources/` decoupled from `db/`):
6	
7	* **IO** — `download_bytes` fetches an object/blob; `read_dataframe` parses it
8	  into pandas. Shared by the column profiler (service layer) and the runner.
9	* **Runner** — `FlatFileCheckRunner` runs GX expectations against the file by
10	  loading it into an in-memory pandas DataFrame and handing that to GX's pandas
11	  datasource, then mapping the result via the shared `gx_runner` machinery. The
12	  `CheckRunner` interface is table-shaped; for a flat-file datasource the
13	  ``table`` argument carries the **file path** and ``schema`` is unused.
14	
15	GX runs entirely in-process on the DataFrame, so — unlike the warehouse runners —
16	the run path is fully testable with a canned frame; only the network download is
17	the deferred-smoke seam.
18	"""
19	
20	from __future__ import annotations
21	
22	import csv
23	import io
24	import re
25	from dataclasses import dataclass
26	from datetime import UTC, datetime
27	from typing import Any, ClassVar
28	
29	import great_expectations as gx
30	
31	from backend.app.core.logging import get_logger
32	from backend.app.core.secrets import SecretStore
33	from backend.app.datasources.adls import AdlsConfig
34	from backend.app.datasources.base import CheckOutcome, CheckSpec, MonitorSpec, SuiteOutcome
35	from backend.app.datasources.gx_runner import run_expectations
36	from backend.app.datasources.monitors import (
37	    FRESHNESS,
38	    VOLUME,
39	    MonitorConfigError,
40	    SafeMonitorError,
41	    freshness_column,
42	    run_monitor_specs,
43	)
44	from backend.app.datasources.s3 import S3Config
45	
46	# Connector timeouts (seconds): fail fast rather than hang the worker thread.
47	# _READ_TIMEOUT is deliberately longer than the SQL profiler's network timeout
48	# (profile_service._NETWORK_TIMEOUT = 30): it covers a full-object download (the
49	# whole CSV/Parquet is pulled before parsing), not a single warehouse query, so a
50	# large file legitimately needs more headroom. Not accidental drift (#147).
51	_CONNECT_TIMEOUT = 10
52	_READ_TIMEOUT = 60
53	
54	log = get_logger(__name__)
55	
56	_FILE_TYPES = {"adls_gen2", "s3"}
57	
58	# Sort floor for files the store reports without a modified time.
59	_MIN_DT = datetime.min.replace(tzinfo=UTC)
60	
61	# Delimiters `sniff_delimiter` will consider, and the fallback when it can't tell
62	# (which is also the pre-#476 behaviour, so a failed sniff never regresses a file
63	# that parses today). Deliberately a short allowlist rather than letting
64	# `csv.Sniffer` pick freely: given a header like `name,title` it will happily
65	# nominate `e` or a space as the delimiter, which is a *worse* silent wrong
66	# answer than assuming a comma.
67	_CSV_DELIMITERS = ",;\t|"
68	_DEFAULT_DELIMITER = ","
69	
70	# How much of the object to hand the sniffer. The header plus a few rows is
71	# plenty and keeps the decode bounded on a large file.
72	_SNIFF_BYTES = 64 * 1024
73	
74	
75	def format_from_path(path: str) -> str | None:
76	    """Infer the file format from the path extension (`None` if unrecognised)."""
77	    lower = path.lower()
78	    if lower.endswith(".csv"):
79	        return "csv"
80	    if lower.endswith((".parquet", ".pq")):
81	        return "parquet"
82	    return None
83	
84	
85	def sniff_delimiter(sample: bytes) -> str:
86	    """Guess a CSV's delimiter from its leading bytes, falling back to a comma.
87	
88	    Pure (no IO) so the decision is testable without a datasource. Sniffing is
89	    per-*file* on purpose: a flat-file connection is a whole bucket/container and
90	    the files under it need not agree on a delimiter, so a per-connection hint
91	    would be the wrong granularity.
92	
93	    Never raises — an undecidable sample (single column, empty file, binary junk)
94	    yields `_DEFAULT_DELIMITER`.
95	    """
96	    text = sample.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
97	    # Sniff over whole lines only: a sample cut mid-row can end in a fragment
98	    # whose field counts don't line up, which is exactly what Sniffer keys off.
99	    head, newline, _ = text.rpartition("\n")
100	    if newline:
101	        text = head
102	    if not text.strip():
103	        return _DEFAULT_DELIMITER
104	    try:
105	        return csv.Sniffer().sniff(text, delimiters=_CSV_DELIMITERS).delimiter
106	    except csv.Error:
107	        return _DEFAULT_DELIMITER
108	
109	
110	def read_csv_bytes(raw: io.BytesIO, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
111	    """`pd.read_csv` over `raw` with the delimiter sniffed from its header (#476).
112	
113	    The single CSV-parsing seam for every flat-file path — runner, profiler,
114	    column lister, schema-drift introspection — so they can never disagree about
115	    what a file's columns are. Extra `kwargs` (``nrows``, ``usecols``, …) pass
116	    straight through; the buffer is rewound before parsing, so callers may hand
117	    over a buffer at any position.
118	    """
119	    import pandas as pd
120	
121	    # `read`, not `getvalue()[:n]`: getvalue copies the ENTIRE buffer before the
122	    # slice, so on a large CSV — which the runner already holds whole in memory —
123	    # picking a delimiter would transiently double peak RSS. The bound is meant to
124	    # cap the work, not just the decode.
125	    raw.seek(0)
126	    sep = sniff_delimiter(raw.read(_SNIFF_BYTES))
127	    raw.seek(0)
128	    return pd.read_csv(raw, sep=sep, **kwargs)
129	
130	
131	def _s3_client(cfg: S3Config, secret: str) -> Any:
132	    """A boto3 S3 client for `cfg` with the standard fail-fast timeouts."""
133	    import boto3
134	    from botocore.config import Config
135	
136	    return boto3.client(
137	        "s3",
138	        region_name=cfg.region,
139	        aws_access_key_id=cfg.access_key_id,
140	        aws_secret_access_key=secret,
141	        config=Config(connect_timeout=_CONNECT_TIMEOUT, read_timeout=_READ_TIMEOUT),
142	    )
143	
144	
145	def _blob_service(acfg: AdlsConfig, secret: str) -> Any:
146	    """An ADLS `BlobServiceClient` for `acfg` (caller must `.close()` it)."""
147	    from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient
148	
149	    return BlobServiceClient(account_url=acfg.account_url, credential=secret)
150

## #900 — a monitor failure could persist a live credential (security)

`monitors.py` stored raw `str(exc)` as a failed check's `error_message`, which flows into `results.observed_value` → the run-detail API → the UI. **That sink never passes the logger-level scrubber** — CLAUDE.md §10's discipline protects logs, not DB columns — and Azure storage exceptions embed the full SAS-signed URL in their text (#828). A failed flat-file monitor could therefore write a working credential into a row any viewer can read.

**The obvious fix was wrong, and the existing tests caught it.** Routing everything through `classify_failure_reason` turned "unknown freshness column `'nope'`" into "The run failed to execute. See the server logs for details." — six tests failed, correctly: a config typo became undiagnosable from the UI. Classification is the right answer for driver text and the wrong answer for messages we wrote ourselves.

So safety is now **declared, not guessed**:

```python
class SafeMonitorError(Exception):
    """Marker: str(exc) is DataQ-authored and safe to persist verbatim."""
```

`MonitorConfigError` and `FlatFileReadError` carry the marker (both construct every message from known-safe parts); anything unmarked is classified. The docstring states the rule for adding to it — *if it can ever interpolate a driver message, a URL, or a connection string, leave it unmarked.*

**Verified against the unfixed code**, per rule 4a: reverting the fix makes both tests fail *for the right reason* — the assertion that trips is `sig=…SECRETSIGNATURE%3D not in message`. The test asserts on the **pipeline**, not the classifier, which is the #849 lesson: testing the scrub helper proves nothing about the path that forgot to call it.

## #306 — a typo'd filter returned a confident empty list

`provider`/`env` flowed straight into the `WHERE`, so `?provider=ADF` (right name, wrong case) returned `200 []` — indistinguishable from "this provider has no runs". Same confidently-empty class as #828.

Now 422 with the allowed values, via `orchestration_service.validate_read_filters` — service layer, mirroring `trigger_binding_service._validate_provider_env` which guards the write path against the same vocabularies. Omitting a filter still means "no filter". The tests seed a real pipeline run first, so an empty body could only come from the filter, never from an empty table.

## #728 — the one hardcoded deploy-target coupling in app code

`allowed_hosts=["*.azurecontainerapps.io", …]` was a literal in `build_mcp_app`, contradicting the ADR 0010/0013 config guardrail: any non-ACA deployment whose proxy forwards a different upstream Host (EKS/GKE, on-prem, a renamed compose service) got a **421 with no way to configure it**. Now `MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, with the ACA-shaped list as the default so existing deployments are byte-identical — pinned by a test, since a silent narrowing here 421s prod.

## #457 — a trip-wire, not a fix

The trigger-dedup partial index's predicate is spelled in **three** places (model `__table_args__`, migration, service `ON CONFLICT`) and each must name every provider. Adding one without widening them is silent: dedup just stops applying to the new provider, so a re-delivered webhook creates a duplicate run. Nothing fails, nothing logs.

dbt was added and the widening **was** done correctly by hand — which is precisely why this is worth pinning: it worked that time, and nothing would have noticed if it hadn't. Nothing else in `monitors.py`'s callers persists raw exception text.

Both endpoints call it with the right argument set (`runs.py:328` provider-only, matching that endpoint's actual params; `runs.py:352` provider+env).

`backend/tests/db/test_orchestration_predicate_drift.py`'s own docstring says the predicate is "spelled in three places — the model's `__table_args__`, the migration that created it, and the service constant." But nothing checks the **migration file** (`backend/alembic/versions/*.py`) or the live Postgres index — `backend/tests/conftest.py:201` builds the test schema via `Base.metadata.create_all(engine)`, not by applying Alembic migrations, so there is no automated check that a hand-written migration's `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE ...` actually matches the model. Import/error-handler wiring, MRO for the `SafeMonitorError` mixins, and the closed-vocabulary sources (`ORCHESTRATION_PROVIDERS`, `ENVS` in `backend/app/db/models.py:99,101`) all check out.

## Result: 89 → 82 open issues, 15 resolved

**Closed on evidence, no code needed (6).** Six agents re-checked 48 candidates against the tree rather than the ticket:

- **#322, #573** — already fixed weeks ago, tracked to completion under *later* duplicates (#640, #714). Verified in-tree and re-ran the specs.
- **#929** — a subset of #787, which now carries a real count: **112 sites across 14 files**, not the filing-time ~93.
- **#893** — warehouse lineage *was* live-verified on both warehouses during the 07-18 arc; the evidence existed only in a ledger paragraph, so I quoted it onto the issue.
- **#731** — findings register discharged (3 of 5 children closed, 2 tracked).
- **#541** — the audit **was** the deliverable: both 500-risk paths are closed, and the three remaining `users.id` FKs are latent by design, with the revisit trigger recorded.

**Shipped (9)** across [#984](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/984) (merged), [#985](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/985), [#986](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/986) — both reviewed, clean, auto-merge armed. [#988](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/988) carries the register update.

## The reviews were worth more than the features

**I broke the SAST gate in #984 and shipped it.** I counted bandit's *warnings* (37 → 0) and called it green — the gate is the **exit code**, which went 0 → 5 findings. The review caught it live. The diagnosis was wrong too: each site had *two* markers, one on the flagged node (load-bearing) and one outside its range (inert), and the `no failed test` warning names the inert one **without saying which is which**. That's now CONTRIBUTING rule 16, and #806's "zero warnings" AC is recorded as the false premise it was — 17 warnings are intrinsic to a marker on a multi-line node.

**#900's obvious fix was wrong and six existing tests said so.** Classifying every exception turned "unknown freshness column `'nope'`" into "the run failed to execute". Safety is now *declared* via a `SafeMonitorError` marker, not guessed.

**Two of my own comments overclaimed** — the #915 field-exclusivity claim (false; → [#987](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/987)) and the #457 guard's three-way coverage claim (it checks two; the migration is never applied in the test schema). ---
name: feedback-prod-no-preexisting-excuse
description: "DataQ is in prod: 'pre-existing' is never a reason to drop a finding — every issue found is fixed or filed, no exceptions"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
---

**Standing instruction (2026-07-25, user):** DataQ is running in production. **"It's
pre-existing" is not a disposition.** Any issue noticed — mine, a reviewer's, an
agent's, a stray diagnostic — must end in one of exactly two states:

1. **Fixed**, in this PR or a follow-up, or
2. **Filed** as a GitHub issue with enough detail to act on.

Never a third: mentioned in a comment, noted in a review reply, buried in a
docstring, or waved off as out of scope. A finding that exists only in prose is
lost the moment the conversation ends.

**Why:** the age of a bug says nothing about its blast radius. In prod, a defect
that predates the change is still live for users right now; "pre-existing" only
describes when it was introduced, not whether it matters. This project has been
burned repeatedly by exactly this — #953 (UC freshness broken since #426, three
green suites), #954 (dead credentials invisible for weeks), #828 (lineage dark
for six days). Every one was "pre-existing" the day before it cost real time.

**What counts as a finding:** a wrong result, a silent failure, a confidently-empty
response, a missing guard, a test that asserts less than its name claims, a
docstring that overclaims, a lint/type diagnostic nobody has triaged. If it took
thought to decide it was fine, that reasoning belongs on an issue too.

**How to apply:**
- Reviewer says "pre-existing, not a blocker" → **file it**, then say so in the PR
  reply with the issue number. Do not merge on the reviewer's leniency.
- Deciding something is genuinely NOT a defect → record the determination and the
  evidence (a PR comment is enough), so nobody re-litigates it. Verified-benign is
  a valid outcome; unexamined is not.
- Documenting a known limitation in a docstring or comment → that is necessary but
  **not sufficient**; the tracked issue is what makes it work rather than folklore.
- Deferring in-PR scope is fine and often right — the follow-up issue is what makes
  it a deferral instead of a drop.

Reinforces [[feedback-review-before-merge]] ("any deferred finding must be
filed/noted, never silently dropped") and CONTRIBUTING rule 3 (defects → issue
first, never silent fixes) — this extends both to findings whose *origin* predates
the change. Mirrored into CONTRIBUTING rule 3a and CLAUDE.md §11.

input.content:
Found by the agentic review on [#986](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/986) (the #900 fix). Documented in the code at the time but **not filed** — filed now under CONTRIBUTING rule 3a, since a limitation that lives only in a docstring is folklore, not tracked work.

## The inconsistency

`#900` established the rule that a monitor's `error_message` is persisted verbatim **only** when the exception is marked `SafeMonitorError`, and the marker's docstring defines the bar as:

> Subclass this **only** when every message the exception can carry is built by DataQ from the user's own configuration (a column name, a numeric range, a monitor kind) or from static text.

`_as_aware_datetime` (`backend/app/datasources/monitors.py`) does not meet that bar:

```python
raise MonitorConfigError(
    f"freshness value from {source} is not a parseable timestamp: {scalar[:40]!r}"
)
```

`scalar` is a **cell value read from the target table** — data, not configuration. `MonitorConfigError` is safe-marked, so this string is persisted verbatim into `results.observed_value` and rendered in the UI.

## Why it is not a live leak

Stated so nobody escalates this beyond its actual severity:

- It is a **freshness column's** value, so by construction the data is a timestamp-ish column — not a credential, not free-text PII.
- The same column's value is already returned as `observed_value` on the **success** path, so a reader of that check can see it anyway. This discloses nothing new to that audience.
- It is truncated to 40 characters.

So the exposure is bounded and arguably justified — you cannot tell a user *which* value is unparseable without showing it. The docstring now says so explicitly.

## Why it is still worth an issue

1. **The invariant is stated more strictly than it is enforced.** The next person adding a `SafeMonitorError` subclass reads a rule that the codebase itself already breaks, which erodes the rule. Either the rule widens (with the widening argued) or this call site changes.
2. **The redaction policy has no say here.** Suites carry a column policy (`column_policy`, #417/#365) that governs failing-sample redaction. This path bypasses it entirely — if a user ever points a freshness monitor at a column they consider sensitive, the redaction machinery that exists for exactly that purpose is not consulted.
3. It is the kind of narrow, reasoned exception that becomes a precedent by accident.

## Options

- **(a)** Drop the value entirely: "…is not a parseable timestamp" plus the column name. Loses diagnosability; the user must query the column themselves.
- **(b)** Keep it, and widen the marker's rule to "config, static text, or a bounded echo of the value under test — justified per site". Honest, but weakens the guarantee.
- **(c)** Route the echo through the suite's column policy, so a column marked sensitive is masked here exactly as it would be in a failing sample. Most consistent with the rest of the product; most work.

(c) is the one that makes the two redaction stories agree.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `SafeMonitorError` rule and every call site agree — either the site changes or the rule does, with the reasoning recorded
- [ ] If the echo stays, a test pins that it is bounded and that a column-policy-sensitive column is handled deliberately (masked or explicitly exempted)
- [ ] No other safe-marked message echoes target data without the same explicit justification (audit the raise sites)

input.content:
Found by the agentic review on [#986](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/986) (the #457 drift guard). Written into the test's docstring at the time but **not filed** — filed now under CONTRIBUTING rule 3a.

## The gap

`#457` added `backend/tests/db/test_orchestration_predicate_drift.py` to stop the trigger-dedup partial index's predicate drifting when a fourth `OrchestrationProvider` is added. The predicate is spelled in **three** places:

1. the model's `Run.__table_args__` `postgresql_where`,
2. the **Alembic migration** that created/widened the index,
3. `orchestration_service._ORCH_TRIGGER_PREDICATE`, used as the `ON CONFLICT` `index_where`.

The guard covers **1 vs 3**, and both against `ORCHESTRATION_PROVIDERS`. It does **not** cover 2, because the test schema is built with `Base.metadata.create_all` (`backend/tests/conftest.py`), not by applying migrations — so the model and the *live* index are never compared anywhere in CI.

## The scenario that survives

Add a provider; widen `ORCHESTRATION_PROVIDERS`, the model predicate and the service predicate correctly; **ship no migration**. Every test is green — the two Python spellings agree with each other and with the vocabulary — while production's index predicate is stale. Dedup then silently stops applying to the new provider, so a re-delivered webhook creates a **duplicate run** instead of being rejected. Nothing fails, nothing logs; you find out from duplicate rows.

That is precisely the failure the guard was written to prevent, which makes the gap worth closing rather than tolerating.

## Why this generalises beyond one index

`create_all`-built test schemas mean **no** model-vs-migration divergence is caught anywhere: a column default, a CHECK constraint, a partial index predicate, an `ondelete` — the ORM metadata is the only thing tests ever see. The `alembic upgrade head` path is exercised by the deploy job and by the E2E lane on a fresh database, but not compared against the model.

The general fix is a migration-parity check: build one schema with `create_all` and another with `alembic upgrade head`, then diff them (Alembic's own `compare_metadata` autogenerate API does this — a non-empty diff means model and migrations disagree). That single test would have caught #913 (a backfill migration targeting `checks.column_policy` when the column lives on `suites`) before it broke every fresh database.

## Options

- **(a) Narrow:** assert the predicate of the live `uq_runs_suite_triggered_by` index after `alembic upgrade head` in a session-scoped fixture. Closes this index only.
- **(b) General (recommended):** one `compare_metadata`-based parity test over the whole schema. Higher value, and it subsumes (a) — the cost is a second schema build in CI and triaging whatever pre-existing drift it surfaces on first run (which is itself worth knowing).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] CI fails when the model's schema and `alembic upgrade head` disagree — at minimum for the partial-index predicate, ideally schema-wide
- [ ] The pre-existing drift the first run surfaces is triaged: each item fixed or filed (rule 3a), not silenced wholesale
- [ ] `test_orchestration_predicate_drift.py`'s docstring caveat is removed once the migration leg is genuinely covered

---
name: dev-closes-keyword-only-closes-the-first
description: "GitHub's Closes keyword auto-closes only the FIRST issue in a comma list — repeat the keyword per issue, and always verify states after merge"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
---

`Closes #563, #601, #915, #916, #949` in a PR body closes **#563 only**. GitHub
parses one issue reference per closing keyword; the remaining comma-separated
numbers become plain links and are ignored **silently** — no warning, no hint in
the merge UI.

**Write it as:** `Closes #563. Closes #601. Closes #915.` — one keyword per issue
(newlines or periods both work). Same for `Fixes`/`Resolves`.

**Then verify, don't assume.** The failure is invisible at merge time, so make the
check part of merging:

```bash
for n in 563 601 915 916 949; do printf "%s=%s " $n "$(gh issue view $n --json state --jq .state)"; done
```

Anything still `OPEN` gets closed by hand with a comment naming the merging PR.

**Seen twice:** the #720 batch (recorded in `docs/progress.md` — "GitHub's `Closes`
keyword only auto-closed #197 as the first item in the comma list") and again on
2026-07-25, where three PRs claimed 13 issues and closed **3**. Knowing about it is
not enough; the verification loop above is what actually catches it.

Why it matters beyond tidiness: the issue register is the project's memory of what
is done. Ten issues silently staying open makes the next triage re-investigate
work that already shipped — which is the same cost as [[feedback-prod-no-preexisting-excuse]]
is trying to avoid from the other direction.

## 1. Standing rule: "pre-existing" is not a disposition

DataQ runs in production, where a defect that predates your change is live for users **right now** — its age describes when it was introduced, not whether it matters. So every finding ends in exactly one of two states: **fixed**, or **filed**. Never a third.

- A reviewer'"'"'s "pre-existing, not a blocker" means *file it and reference the number*, not *merge past it*.
- Concluding something is genuinely **not** a defect is a valid outcome — record the determination and evidence so nobody re-litigates it. **Verified-benign is fine; unexamined is not.**
- A docstring note is necessary but **not sufficient**; the tracked issue is what keeps it work rather than folklore.

Landed as CONTRIBUTING **rule 3a** and a CLAUDE.md §11 entry, cited to the three incidents that were all "pre-existing" the day before they cost real time: #953 (UC freshness broken since #426, behind three green suites), #954 (dead credentials invisible until a run failed), #828 (lineage dark for six days).

- **#990** — **model-vs-migration schema parity is never checked anywhere.** The test schema is `create_all`, so #457'"'"'s guard covers 2 of 3 predicate spellings. The same gap is what let #913'"'"'s mistargeted backfill migration break every fresh database.

## 2. A real register bug this session caused

**Three merged PRs claimed 13 issues and closed 3.** GitHub honours only the **first** issue after a `Closes` keyword; the rest of a comma-separated list are ignored **silently** — no warning at merge, nothing in the UI.

CLOSING SEVERAL ISSUES? Repeat the keyword for EACH one:
    Fixes #1. Fixes #2. Fixes #3.
After merging, VERIFY rather than assume:
    for n in 1 2 3; do gh issue view $n --json state --jq .state; done
```

All ten closed by hand, each with its merging PR named.

content.content:
## What happened (2026-07-18, prod)

The 00:10Z deploy (SHA `4f8b2ae0`, run 29622325290) rolled the worker at 00:12. The new replica booted normally — tasks registered, redis connected, `celery ready`, `beat: Starting...` at 00:12:37 — then, after a **transient broker disconnect at 00:13:02** (`consumer: Connection to broker lost. Trying to re-establish the connection...`, normal roll-time churn; Redis itself was healthy the whole time, up since 07-12 with 0 restarts) and one `missed heartbeat` line at 00:13:05, the process went **completely silent for 6 hours**:

- zero beat ticks (a healthy embedded beat logs `Scheduler: Sending due task` every 60s),
- zero task receipts, zero reconnect retries, zero exceptions,
- replica `Running`, restartCount 0, App Insights worker traces frozen at 00:13:05.

Blast radius: scheduled-suite dispatch, ADF/Airflow/dbt orchestration polling, gap recovery, and the retention purge were all dead 00:13→06:17Z. `az containerapp revision restart` at 06:17 fully restored it — beat started and `recover_orchestration_gaps` ran immediately (3 connections swept).

**Stranded side-effect:** the post-deploy harness smoke's `pl_flow_a_orders` run (Succeeded in ADF at 00:19Z) fell outside both `_POLL_LOOKBACK` (15m) and the gap-recovery window (1h) by the time the worker was revived — `recorded: 0`, exactly the #828-documented backlog gap. Not re-produced (the pipeline itself succeeded; the binding path was already live-verified 07-13); noted here so the ledger stays honest.

## Why this is a class, not a one-off

This is the third "worker looks alive but does nothing" incident (#852 exporter starvation, #854 unbounded row-lock wait, now a wedged broker-reconnect). Each had a different cause; all shared the same failure surface: **the embedded beat has no liveness signal**, so the platform's `Running` state and the app's own logs both report health while every periodic responsibility is dead. Detection was manual each time.

## Suggested fixes (defense in depth)

1. **Beat liveness you can probe**: beat heartbeat file/redis key bumped per tick + a Container Apps liveness probe (or the #841 `HealthPublisher` path) that fires when the bump goes stale for N minutes. This catches ALL members of the class regardless of cause.
2. **Reconnect must be loud and bounded**: investigate why the kombu/celery re-establish loop after the 00:13:02 disconnect neither retried-with-logs nor raised — pin `broker_connection_retry_on_startup` / heartbeat settings so a wedged reconnect dies (and the replica restarts) instead of hanging forever. A crash-looping worker is strictly better than a silent one.
3. **The DB-truth alert already proposed in #843's family**: `last_polled_at` staleness across ALL connections is the one signal that cannot lie (the #852 lesson) — alert on it workspace-wide, not per-connection.

## Evidence
- Worker console: boot banner ends 00:13:05Z; next line is `beat: Starting...` 06:17:32Z (post-restart).
- App Insights: `traces | summarize max(timestamp) by cloud_RoleName` → dataq-worker frozen at 00:13:05Z (850 boot-window records, then nothing).
- The restart + recovery: `recover_orchestration_gaps` received/succeeded 06:17:32Z (`{'connections': 3, 'recorded': 0, ...}`).

"""Beat liveness watchdog — kill a worker that is alive but doing nothing (#904).

Three times now (2026-07-18 00:12Z, the #905 six-hour outage, 2026-07-19 04:55Z)
a post-deploy roll has left the worker in the same state: the container reports
Healthy, Celery logs ``ready`` and ``beat: Starting...``, no exception is raised
— and **not one scheduled task ever executes**. Orchestration polling, scheduled
runs, gap recovery, the reaper and the purge all stop silently. Every single
time, the only thing that told the truth was the DATABASE (``last_polled_at``
frozen), and every single time the fix was a human noticing and restarting the
revision.

This module makes the system notice instead.

**What is measured.** A periodic task writes a timestamp on *execution*

by a concrete failure mode found in review:

94	## 4. Datasources vs orchestration — critical distinction
95	
96	**Datasources** are stores you write DQ checks against:
97	- Snowflake (DEV/QA/UAT)
98	- ADLS Gen2 (flat files)
99	- AWS S3 (flat files)
100	- Unity Catalog / Databricks
101	- Apache Iceberg (native `pyiceberg` read — ADR 0030; engine-registered Iceberg tables also work zero-code under the `snowflake`/`unity_catalog` connections)
102	
103	**Orchestration providers** are NOT datasources. They are workflow engines whose pipelines/DAGs we observe and react to. Their *only* three responsibilities in DataQ:
104	
105	1. **Monitor** pipeline/DAG runs → stored in `pipeline_runs` table (separate from `runs` / `results`).
106	2. **Detect failure** in near-real-time via provider-specific event channels (webhook for both).
107	3. **Trigger suite execution on successful completion** via `trigger_bindings` (`provider`, `pipeline_or_dag_id`, `suite_id`, `env`). Failure events alert the user but do NOT trigger suite runs.
108	
109	All three providers implement a single `OrchestrationProvider` interface — ADF is the reference implementation, Airflow is the second, dbt (ADR 0029) is the third (artifact-poll + HMAC callback, no host REST API). **Never hardcode ADF-only logic; always go through the abstraction.**
110	
111	| Provider | Event channel | Auth | Polling fallback |
112	|---|---|---|---|
113	| ADF | Azure Monitor alert → webhook | Shared secret header (Azure Monitor's only mode) | ADF REST API, 10 min |
114	| Airflow | DAG `on_*_callback` → webhook | HMAC-signed payload (signing key in Key Vault) | Airflow REST API `dagRuns`, 10 min |
115	| dbt | post-build callback → webhook | HMAC-signed payload (app-level signing key) | poll `run_results.json` artifact (adls/s3/file), 10 min |
116	
117	Airflow callbacks require the user to add a snippet to their DAGs (we can't mutate them). Polling is the documented fallback.
118	
119	**Anti-pattern (do not do this):** treating ADF/Airflow as a 5th/6th datasource in the connection editor, check editor, or suite model.
120

124	
125	- **v1:** Great Expectations (GX Core) is the sole DQ framework across all datasources. Unifies result schema, suite/check model, MCP tools, and the check editor. Every v1 check is a GX **expectation** (`check.kind = 'expectation'`).
126	- **v1.1+:** platform-native engines are **connection-anchored** (ADR [0036](docs/adr/0036-connection-anchored-check-engines.md)): every datasource connection offers GX; a Snowflake connection additionally offers **DMF**, Unity Catalog offers **DQX** (DLT/streaming — GX is batch-only), a future BigQuery type offers **Dataplex**. Engine selection is **per check** (`check.engine`, default `gx`, validated against the connection's capability set; `kind` stays orthogonal to `engine`) — supersedes the earlier suite-level `engine: gx | dqx` toggle sketch. DMF is the first native build; DQX/Dataplex are trigger-gated (see the ADR §6).

Verified against the tree and against the running prod app, not against the ticket.

### Item 1 (beat liveness) — shipped and live in production

\`backend/app/worker/beat_watchdog.py\` exists (landed via #904/#931) and implements exactly what this issue asked for, with a better design than the one proposed here:

- The heartbeat is written on task **execution**, not by the scheduler. That is the crucial detail — a scheduler-written heartbeat \"would have reported healthy right through the outage\", since the failure mode is *beat keeps queueing, nothing consumes*.
- It kills the process instead of exposing an HTTP probe, because the worker serves neither HTTP nor TCP and \"dying is portable\".
- Five guards, each earned by a review finding: boot grace, never-kill-on-unreadable-store, never-kill-on-a-predecessor's-stamp, never-kill-while-tasks-run, and consecutive confirmations.

**Confirmed live in prod**, not just merged: the deployed worker image \`dff6d958\` contains the module (\`git cat-file -e dff6d958:backend/app/worker/beat_watchdog.py\`), and \`az containerapp show\` returns **no** \`BEAT_*\` env override, so the defaults apply — \`beat_watchdog_stale_after_s=600\` (>0 = enabled). The class fix this issue asked for is running.

### Item 2 (loud, bounded reconnect) — the proposed fix is a no-op; the real cause needs reproduction

I started to implement it and stopped, because the specific suggestion does not hold:

- **\`health_check_interval\` is already set.** \`kombu.transport.redis.DEFAULT_HEALTH_CHECK_INTERVAL = 25\` (kombu 5.6.2), applied by default. Adding it to \`broker_transport_options\` would change nothing while looking like a fix — the #974 class of change (a \"bump\" whose diff moves no resolution).
- **Retries are already bounded.** Celery's \`broker_connection_max_retries\` defaults to a finite value, so retry *exhaustion* is not the mechanism either.
- **The incident log rules both out anyway:** it records **zero reconnect retries**. The retry loop never ran. That points at a read with no timeout hanging below the retry machinery — the #854 forever-wait shape — not at retry policy.

Setting a broker \`socket_timeout\` is the candidate mechanism, but it interacts with how kombu's redis transport polls for messages, and a wrong value risks breaking task consumption in production. **That is not a change to guess-ship against a live deployment on the strength of a plausible story.** It needs the wedge reproduced (kill the Redis TCP connection out from under a consumer and observe) before a value is chosen.

### Item 3 (DB-truth staleness alert) — still open, overlaps #843

Unchanged. \`last_polled_at\` staleness across ALL connections remains the signal that cannot lie.

### Suggested re-scope

Item 1 is done. **The severity of this issue has genuinely dropped**: the outage it describes now self-heals, because the watchdog restarts the worker instead of a human noticing six hours later. What remains is hardening (item 2, needs a reproduction) and alerting (item 3, overlaps #843) — worth keeping open, but no longer P1-as-filed.

input.new_string:
def list_pipeline_runs(
    session: Session,
    *,
    provider: str | None = None,
    status: str | None = None,
    limit: int = 50,
    offset: int = 0,
) -> list[PipelineRun]:
    """Monitored orchestrator pipeline/DAG runs, newest first, with paging (#928).

    Optionally filtered by ``provider`` and/or ``status``.

    **The `id` tie-break is load-bearing, not tidiness.** `created_at` alone is not
    a total order — the poll ingests a batch inside one transaction, so Postgres'
    transaction-scoped `now()` gives every row in that batch an identical
    timestamp. Under `LIMIT/OFFSET` a non-total order lets the database return
    tied rows in any order per query, so the same row can appear on two pages
    while another is never returned at all. Paging without this is worse than no
    paging: it looks complete and silently isn't (the same nondeterminism #889
    fixed for latest-run-per-suite).
    """
    stmt = (
        select(PipelineRun)
        .order_by(PipelineRun.created_at.desc(), PipelineRun.id.desc())
        .limit(limit)
        .offset(offset)
    )
    if provider is not None:
        stmt = stmt.where(PipelineRun.provider == provider)
    if status is not None:
        stmt = stmt.where(PipelineRun.status == status)
    return list(session.scalars(stmt))

def test_list_pipeline_runs_pages_with_offset(client: TestClient, db_session: Any) -> None:
    """`offset` actually pages, and never returns the same row twice (#928).

    Before this, `offset` was not a parameter at all — FastAPI silently discarded
    it, so a paging client re-read page 1 forever while believing it was advancing.
    """
    owner = _user(db_session, "owner@ex")
    for _ in range(5):
        _pipeline_run(db_session, owner, provider="adf", status="succeeded")
    _as(owner)

    page1 = client.get("/api/v1/pipeline_runs?limit=2&offset=0").json()
    page2 = client.get("/api/v1/pipeline_runs?limit=2&offset=2").json()
    page3 = client.get("/api/v1/pipeline_runs?limit=2&offset=4").json()

    assert [len(page1), len(page2), len(page3)] == [2, 2, 1]
    ids = [p["id"] for p in page1 + page2 + page3]
    assert len(set(ids)) == 5, "paging returned a duplicate row"
    # And the pages together are the whole set, in order — no row skipped.
    everything = [p["id"] for p in client.get("/api/v1/pipeline_runs?limit=200").json()]
    assert ids == everything


def test_list_pipeline_runs_ordering_is_total_so_paging_cannot_skip(
    client: TestClient, db_session: Any
) -> None:
    """Rows sharing a `created_at` must still have a deterministic order (#928).

    This is the case that makes paging sound or unsound. The poll ingests a batch
    inside ONE transaction, and Postgres' `now()` is transaction-scoped — so a
    real batch lands with identical timestamps. Ordering by `created_at` alone
    then lets the database return tied rows in any order per query, and
    `LIMIT/OFFSET` over a non-total order silently drops some rows while
    repeating others.

    These rows are written in a single transaction precisely to reproduce that
    tie, and the assertion is that paging still enumerates the set exactly once.
    """
    owner = _user(db_session, "owner@ex")
    tied = datetime(2026, 7, 1, tzinfo=UTC)
    for _ in range(6):
        pr = _pipeline_run(db_session, owner, provider="adf", status="succeeded")
        pr.created_at = tied  # same instant for every row
    db_session.commit()
    _as(owner)

    seen: list[str] = []
    for offset in (0, 2, 4):
        seen += [p["id"] for p in client.get(f"/api/v1/pipeline_runs?limit=2&offset={offset}").json()]

    assert len(seen) == 6
    assert len(set(seen)) == 6, "tied timestamps let paging return a row twice"

def test_list_pipeline_runs_ordering_is_total_so_paging_cannot_skip(
    client: TestClient, db_session: Any
) -> None:
    """Rows sharing a `created_at` must still have a deterministic order (#928).

    This is the case that makes paging sound or unsound. The poll ingests a batch
    inside ONE transaction, and Postgres' `now()` is transaction-scoped — so a
    real batch lands with identical timestamps. Ordering by `created_at` alone
    then lets the database return tied rows in any order per query, and
    `LIMIT/OFFSET` over a non-total order silently drops some rows while
    repeating others.

    These rows are written in a single transaction precisely to reproduce that
    tie, and the assertion is that paging still enumerates the set exactly once.
    """
    owner = _user(db_session, "owner@ex")
    tied = datetime(2026, 7, 1, tzinfo=UTC)
    for pr in _pipeline_runs_on_one_connection(db_session, owner, count=6):
        pr.created_at = tied  # same instant for every row, as a real batch lands
    db_session.commit()
    _as(owner)

    seen: list[str] = []
    for offset in (0, 2, 4):
        seen += [
            p["id"] for p in client.get(f"/api/v1/pipeline_runs?limit=2&offset={offset}").json()
        ]

    assert len(seen) == 6
    assert len(set(seen)) == 6, "tied timestamps let paging return a row twice"

def test_pipeline_run_ordering_is_total_so_paging_cannot_skip() -> None:
    """The paging order must be TOTAL — it ends in a unique column (#928).

    Why this is a structural assertion and not a behavioural one, stated because
    the behavioural version is tempting and worthless: the poll ingests a batch in
    ONE transaction and Postgres' `now()` is transaction-scoped, so real batches
    land with identical `created_at`. Ordering by that alone is not a total order,
    and `LIMIT/OFFSET` over a non-total order may return a row on two pages while
    never returning another.

    *May.* Postgres is free to vary the order of tied rows but is not obliged to,
    and in practice a small table with a stable plan returns them consistently. A
    test that pages tied rows and asserts no duplicates therefore **passes against
    the unfixed code** most of the time — verified: removing the `id` tie-break
    left that test green. That is the #948 coin-flip lesson exactly, so this
    asserts the invariant itself rather than waiting for the database to misbehave
    on cue.
    """
    from backend.app.db.models import PipelineRun as PR

    order = orchestration_service.pipeline_run_order_by()
    # The last key must be a unique column, or ties have no defined resolution.
    assert order[-1].element is PR.id.__clause_element__()
    assert len(order) >= 2, "a single non-unique sort key cannot be a total order"

fix(api): page GET /pipeline_runs, with a total order so paging is sound

`GET /api/v1/pipeline_runs` capped at 200 with no `offset` parameter at all.
FastAPI silently discards unknown query params, so `?offset=200` returned 200 OK
and re-read page 1 — a paging loop "counted" 20,200 rows against a table holding
211. Beyond the newest 200, the history was unreachable with no indication it had
been truncated.

Adds `offset` (matching the `/assets` shape) AND an `id` tie-break on the
ordering. The tie-break is not tidiness: the poll ingests a batch inside one
transaction and Postgres' now() is transaction-scoped, so real batches land with
identical created_at. LIMIT/OFFSET over a non-total order may return a row on two
pages and never return another — paging that looks complete and silently isn't,
which is worse than no paging.

The ordering is asserted STRUCTURALLY, not behaviourally, and the reason is
recorded in both the code and the test: Postgres is free to vary the order of
tied rows but not obliged to, so a test that pages tied rows and checks for
duplicates passes against the unfixed code whenever the plan happens to be
stable. Verified — that version of the test stayed green with the tie-break
removed. It is the #948 coin-flip lesson, so the test now asserts the invariant
itself (the final sort key is a unique column).

Both tests verified to fail against the unfixed code, each for its own reason.

Fixes #928

## The bug

`GET /api/v1/pipeline_runs` took `limit` (max 200) and had **no `offset` parameter at all**. FastAPI silently discards unknown query params, so `?offset=200` returned `200 OK` and re-read page 1. A client paging through the set received page 1 forever — the reporter hit exactly this, "counting" 20,200 rows against a table holding 211.

Beyond the newest 200 rows, orchestration history was simply unreachable, with nothing indicating it had been truncated.

## The part that is easy to get wrong

Adding `offset` alone would have produced paging that **looks** complete and silently is not.

The poll ingests a batch inside **one transaction**, and Postgres'"'"' `now()` is transaction-scoped — so a real batch of pipeline runs lands with **identical `created_at`**. Ordering by that column alone is not a total order, and `LIMIT/OFFSET` over a non-total order may hand back the same row on two pages while never returning another. So this adds an `id` tie-break, the same fix #889 made for latest-run-per-suite.

## Why the ordering test is structural, not behavioural

I wrote the behavioural version first — seed rows with tied timestamps, page them, assert no duplicates. **It passed with the tie-break removed.**

Postgres is *free* to vary the order of tied rows but is not *obliged* to; on a small table with a stable plan it returns them consistently. So that test would have been a coin flip dressed as a regression guard — the #948 lesson exactly, which this repo has already paid for once.

The invariant is therefore asserted directly: the ordering ends in a **unique column**. That is precisely what "total order" means, it is stated as a property rather than as one specific column, and it fails immediately if anyone drops the tie-break.

## Verification

Each test was run against deliberately broken code, and each fails for its **own** reason:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `.offset(offset)` removed | `test_list_pipeline_runs_pages_with_offset` **fails** |
| `id` tie-break removed | `test_pipeline_run_ordering_is_total_so_paging_cannot_skip` **fails** |

One test-infrastructure note worth recording: the existing `_pipeline_run` helper mints a **new connection per call**, which trips `uq_connections_orchestrator_type_env` on the second row (an orchestrator is singular per `(type, env)`). Paging tests need several runs, so they share one connection — which is also the more faithful shape, since real pipeline runs all hang off one.

## Scope

This closes #928'"'"'s paging AC. The issue'"'"'s second point — that a *silently ignored unknown param* is its own defect class — is broader than this endpoint (it is FastAPI-wide behaviour) and is deliberately not addressed here.

Observed on `main` at `8d4d78a6` (run [30152438827](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/actions/runs/30152438827)) — the **Backend — tests** job failed before running a single test:

```
Error response from daemon: Get "https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/":
  net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
... (retried) ...
Error response from daemon: Get "https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/": context deadline exceeded
```

The job never reached pytest — GitHub's `services:` containers could not be pulled. A re-run went green with no code change, confirming it is transport, not test.

## Why this is filed rather than shrugged off

Filed under CONTRIBUTING rule 3a: an infrastructure flake that **fails a required merge gate** is a real problem, not weather.

1. **It red-flags `main`.** A failure here is indistinguishable at a glance from a genuine regression, so every one costs an investigation — this one cost mine. Worse, it trains the reflex "CI failed, just re-run it", which is exactly how a real failure gets re-run away.
2. **It is unauthenticated Docker Hub.** Four `services:` images across two jobs (`postgres:16-alpine` ×2, `redis:7-alpine` ×2 — `ci.yml:129,143,304,317`) are pulled anonymously on every run. Anonymous pulls are rate-limited and throttled per source IP, and GitHub-hosted runners share egress addresses — so this gets *more* likely as the org's CI volume grows, not less.
3. There is **no retry** on the `services:` pull. GitHub does not retry it, and the job dies immediately.

## Options

1. **Pull through GHCR** — the repo already publishes to GHCR and authenticates there for the Deploy workflow, so mirroring `postgres:16-alpine` / `redis:7-alpine` into `ghcr.io/theurgicduke771/*` costs one scheduled sync job and removes Docker Hub from the merge path entirely. Most robust.
2. **Authenticate the Docker Hub pull** — `docker/login-action` with a token raises the rate limit substantially. Cheapest change; still leaves an external dependency in the gate.
3. **Drop `services:` and start the containers in a step** with an explicit retry loop. Most control, most YAML.

Option 1 aligns with the Redis-7 pin being a deliberate security gate ([#980](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/980)) — controlling where that image comes from is the same concern as controlling its version.

## Note on the pinned versions

Whatever is chosen must preserve `redis:7-alpine` exactly. Per #980 the 7.x pin is a **security gate**, not a staleness artefact — Redis 8 bundles Vector Sets, an unpatched RCE surface. A mirror or registry swap must not quietly become a version bump.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The backend/E2E test jobs no longer depend on an unauthenticated Docker Hub pull
- [ ] `redis:7-alpine` and `postgres:16-alpine` remain the exact versions in use (#980 gate intact)
- [ ] A registry hiccup either retries or fails with a message that is obviously infrastructure, so it is never mistaken for a regression

content.text:
**main is green.** Here's where things stand.

## Broken from this session — found and fixed

Two things, neither of which announced itself:

1. **10 of 13 issues never closed.** Three merged PRs used `Closes #a, #b, #c`; GitHub honours only the **first** issue after the keyword and drops the rest silently. Work had shipped while the register said otherwise. All ten closed by hand, and — since this repo had *already recorded* the same trap on the #720 batch — the countermeasure is now structural rather than memorial: the **PR template** carries the one-keyword-per-issue rule plus the post-merge `gh issue view` verification loop. I then ran that loop over all 21 issues claimed today: **every one verified CLOSED**.

2. **main CI went red** on the #928 merge — Docker Hub timed out pulling CI service containers. Re-run is green. Not code, but filed as **#993**: four `services:` images are pulled *unauthenticated* on every run, there's no retry, and a red main is indistinguishable at a glance from a real regression — which is how the "just re-run it" reflex gets trained.

## The rule, recorded three places

CONTRIBUTING **rule 3a** + CLAUDE.md §11 + memory: *"pre-existing" is not a disposition.* Every finding ends **fixed or filed** — never in a review reply or a docstring. Verified-benign is a valid outcome **if the determination is recorded**; unexamined is not.

I discharged it against my own session first, filing two things I'd written into code comments today and never filed: **#989** (`SafeMonitorError` echoes a target cell value, which its own rule forbids) and **#990** (**model-vs-migration schema parity is never checked anywhere** — the test schema is `create_all`, which is also what let #913's mistargeted migration break every fresh database).

## Work shipped

**#928** — `/pipeline_runs` had no `offset` at all; FastAPI silently discarded it, so a paging client re-read page 1 forever. Fixed with paging **and** an `id` tie-break.

That tie-break is the part worth flagging: I wrote the behavioural test first — seed tied timestamps, page, assert no duplicates — and **it passed with the tie-break removed**. Postgres may vary the order of tied rows but isn't obliged to. It was a coin flip dressed as a regression guard, the #948 lesson again. The invariant is now asserted structurally, and both tests are verified to fail against broken code for their own distinct reasons.

**#905** got a substantive triage instead of a fix, deliberately. Item 1 (beat liveness) is **already shipped and live in prod** — verified in the deployed image with no env override disabling it. Item 2's suggested fix would have been a **no-op**: kombu already defaults `health_check_interval = 25`. I stopped rather than ship a placebo against a live deployment; the real mechanism needs the wedge reproduced.

## Register

**89 → 70 open** (43 in `v1.1 Backlog`), **0 open PRs**, main green.

One thing needs your decision: **#900's credential fix is merged but not deployed** — prod still runs `dff6d958` from 07-19. Deploys are manual and now cost real money. Want me to run the Deploy workflow?

No — only a handful are genuinely blocked. Here's the honest split of the 70.

## Actually blocked — 5

| Issue | Blocker | Verified |
|---|---|---|
| #969 | eslint's transitive `minimatch@3` must go first | Today: still in the lockfile |
| #970 | `azure-monitor-opentelemetry-exporter` must support OTel 1.44 | Today: latest is still `1.0.0b55`, pinned `~1.43` |
| #717 | pyiceberg v3 read path not GA | Today: already on latest `0.11.1` |
| #505 | Needs a target cloud subscription that doesn't exist | — |
| #980 | Standing tripwire — nothing to do until someone proposes a Redis 8 bump | — |

## Waiting on **you**, not on code — 4

**#588 / #590** are decided (keep a month) — they're calendar items for ~08-25, not blocked. **#310** needs an ADR decision on history/audit strategy before any code. **#732** is a marketplace checklist with product calls in it. Plus **#597**, the cycle epic — a tracker, not work.

## Deliberately sequenced features — ~34

The W5 slate (#593, #594, #568, #424, #349, #345, #283, #351), W6 (#595, #755, #323, #327, #278, #318), W7 compliance (#431–#435) and stretch (#466, #529, #244), plus the umbrella builds you scoped as ADRs: **OTP** (#734–#738), **RBAC** (#740–#744), **DMF engine** (#895), **tagging** (#888).

These aren't blocked — you chose the order. Any of them could start today.

## Actionable right now, nothing in the way — ~27

This is the bucket I under-sold earlier, and I want to correct it plainly: **in the sweep I labelled things "REAL WORK", which meant "not a 30-minute quick win" — not "can't be done."** Those two got conflated in my summary.

- **Prod reliability:** #954 (dead datasource credential invisible), #838 (warn before expiry), #842/#843 (alerting sweep blocking + delivery-driven edges), #748 (migration-lock runbook remainder), #905 items 2–3
- **Correctness/UX:** #987, #925 (asset browse paging), #947 (MCP N+1), #936 (3-part quoting), #788, #912
- **Unbounded reads** (#854 class): #882, #942, #943
- **Test/CI integrity:** #993 (I filed today), #990 (I filed today), #787 (112 sites), #898, #278
- **Refactors:** #682, #727, #685, #784, #976, #989, #919

If I were picking, the top three by prod value are **#954** (credential blindness — it cost us real time this session), **#993** (a red main indistinguishable from a regression), and **#990** (model-vs-migration parity, the gap that let #913 break every fresh database).

def test_list_suites_query_count_does_not_grow_with_suite_count(
    db_session: Any, monkeypatch: Any
) -> None:
    """`list_suites` must issue a FIXED number of queries, not O(suites) (#947).

    Asserted by counting SQL statements, because the obvious test — "the output
    is still correct" — passes just as happily with the N+1 in place. Only the
    query count distinguishes the two, and an LLM calling this tool cannot see
    the cost, so nothing else would ever surface a regression.

    Three per-suite queries used to run in the loop (connection, check count,
    latest run), so a 30-suite workspace issued ~90 round trips.
    """
    from sqlalchemy import event

    user = _user(db_session)
    for _ in range(4):
        suite = _suite(db_session, user)
        db_session.add(Check(suite_id=suite.id, name="c", expectation_type="expect_x", config={}))
    db_session.commit()
    _as(monkeypatch, db_session, user)

    statements: list[str] = []

    def _record(_conn: Any, _cursor: Any, statement: str, *_rest: Any) -> None:
        statements.append(statement)

    event.listen(db_session.bind, "before_cursor_execute", _record)
    try:
        out = server.list_suites()
    finally:
        event.remove(db_session.bind, "before_cursor_execute", _record)

    assert len(out) == 4
    assert {o["check_count"] for o in out} == {1}, "batching must not lose per-suite counts"
    # 4 suites, and the whole tool stays in single digits. The pre-fix code issued
    # 3 per suite on top of the listing, so this trips immediately if the loop
    # regains a query — while leaving room for the shared prelude to change.
    assert len(statements) <= 8, f"expected a fixed query count, issued {len(statements)}"

The issue named the per-suite latest-run query. Reading the loop, **all three** queries inside it were per-suite:

| Per suite | Now |
|---|---|
| `session.get(Connection, ...)` | one batched `IN` |
| `count()` of checks | one `GROUP BY` |
| latest `Run` | the shared `rollup.latest_runs_per_suite_stmt` |

A 30-suite workspace issued roughly **90 round trips** for a single tool call. This is the worst place in the app to hide an N+1: an LLM calls `list_suites` constantly and has no way to perceive the cost.

## The tie-break comes free, and matters

`get_suite_results` had a **fourth** hand-rolled spelling of "the latest run" (`ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1`). Both call sites now use the shared statement, which carries the `id` tie-break from #889 — so the MCP surface agrees with the dashboard and the asset view about which run is newest when two share a `created_at`, rather than resolving it arbitrarily. The obvious test — assert the output is still right — **passes just as happily with the N+1 in place**, because the output is identical. Only the query count distinguishes them, and nothing else would ever surface a regression on a tool whose caller cannot see latency.

fix(ui): show the tier note on a source that is both degraded and failing

`last_error` and `degraded_reason` are not mutually exclusive: the success path
records the tier note and `_record_refresh_error` never clears it, so a source
that answered coarsely and has since started failing carries both. The #915
split routed such a row to the failing advisory, which showed only the error.

I filed this expecting the fix to be "null the stale tier on failure". Reading
the code says otherwise: `degraded_reason` describes WHICH TIER the source can
answer at — a property of its edition and grants (#902) — not an observation
that decays. It still holds while refreshes fail, so nulling it would discard a
durable fact and leave the user wondering why the graph was thin even before it
went stale. The UI shows both instead, with failure still dominant.

gh pr create --title "fix(ui): show the tier note on a source that is both degraded and failing (#987)" --milestone "v1.1 Week 5 — anomaly monitor kind + metric trends" --body 'Closes #987, which I filed earlier today off the #985 review.

## The bug

`last_error` and `degraded_reason` are **not** mutually exclusive. `warehouse_refresh` sets `degraded_reason` on a successful coarse refresh, and `_record_refresh_error` sets `last_error` without clearing it — so a source that answered coarsely and has since started failing carries both. The #915 split routes that row to the failing advisory, which rendered only the error.

## I filed this with the wrong fix in mind

The issue proposed nulling the stale tier on failure, and called that the better option. **Reading the code says otherwise.**

`degraded_reason` is not a decaying observation — it records **which tier the source is able to answer at**, derived from its edition and grants (#902). That does not stop being true because one refresh failed. Nulling it would throw away a durable fact and leave the user unable to see why the graph was already thin *before* it went stale.

So the fix is the option I ranked second: show both, with failure still dominant (warning severity, error as the headline, tier as a secondary line).

Worth recording because the ordering was only obvious from the code, not from the symptom — which is the whole argument for reading before choosing.

## Test

New case seeds a source with **both** fields and asserts:
- severity stays `ant-alert-warning` — failure still dominates;
- both the error text and the tier note render;
- the source is **not** also listed under the degraded advisory, which would read as two sources with two different problems.

**Verified to fail with the added branch removed.**

## Test plan

- [x] `npx tsc --noEmit` · `pnpm lint` · `pnpm format:check` — clean
- [x] `pnpm test:coverage` — **625 passed / 78 files**, lines **89.97%**
- [x] New test proven to fail against the unfixed component

Fixes #987
